extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, historians, media ethicists, and practicing journalists interested in the history and norms of news reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and identify the objectivity norm in American journalism: its core features, how its presence can be measured, the practices associated with it (e.g., interviewing, wire service use), and the social conditions that produced its articulation in the early 20th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity norm (core features)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objectivity norm guides journalists to separate facts from values and to report only the facts. Objective reporting is supposed to be cool rather than emotional in tone; it takes pains to represent fairly each leading side in a political controversy. According to the norm, the journalist’s job is reporting something called 'news' without commenting on it, slanting it, or shaping its formulation in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity is simultaneously a moral ideal, a set of reporting and editing practices, and an observable pattern of news writing. The norm is upheld specifically against partisan journalism (which rejects inaccuracy but presents information from a party perspective). Anti-patterns: emotional tone, editorializing, explicit partisan advocacy, shaping facts to fit a factional line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of presence of objectivity (four detection modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity’s presence can be identified by several measures: (a) journalists' expressed allegiance to the norm in speeches, conferences, codes of ethics, textbooks, debates and opinion surveys; (b) ethnographers' observations of newsroom routines and adherence to practices; (c) content analysis of newspapers and broadcasts measuring impersonality and non-partisanship; and (d) resistance displayed by adherents when the norm is openly challenged or criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple methods to assess whether objectivity operates as a norm: discourse (codes, speeches), practice (ethnography), text (content analysis), and social reaction (defensive responses by journalists). Each mode supplies distinct evidence and together they indicate whether objectivity functions as a moral/occupational rule rather than merely a stylistic habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, truthfulness, accuracy, and impartiality (professional code elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional ethical elements promoted by journalism organizations (e.g., ASNE's Canons) include 'Sincerity, Truthfulness, Accuracy' and 'Impartiality' as core principles to guide journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These codified principles (adopted by national organizations in the 1920s) are explicit articulations of the objectivity norm; they function as pedagogical tools and public professions of occupational virtue. Examples: Kent Cooper's 1925 creed emphasizing fact-based reporting. In practice, these principles are invoked to justify routines and to signal professional legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical fairness and procedural fairness (modern objectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern objectivity as 'analytical and procedural fairness' crystallized in the 1920s: analytical fairness means separating facts and values and giving balanced analytic treatment; procedural fairness refers to routinized, impartial procedures for newsgathering and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical fairness requires reporters to adopt fact-centered analytic frames; procedural fairness requires institutionalized practices (e.g., sourcing norms, editorial procedures) that produce balanced coverage. Together these distinguish modern objectivity from earlier informal or rhetorical notions of fairness. Scoring: examine both the framing/analysis in copy (analytical) and the documented/newsgathering procedures followed (procedural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stenographic fairness (19th-century speed-and-accuracy ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 19th-century conception emphasizing speed and accuracy of news-gathering (driven by rotary/steam presses and penny papers) — termed 'stenographic fairness' — focused on rapid, accurate transmission of events but coexisted with strong partisan selection and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form values factual transmission and timeliness but does not necessarily imply nonpartisanship; anti-pattern: claiming factual speed/accuracy while omitting or selectively covering opponents' events. Historical caution: speed/accuracy practices can be compatible with partisan editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing and note-taking as objective practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing (emerging widely 1870s–1900s) became a central reporting practice oriented to audiences and to making stories rather than promoting party lines; by the 1920s, textbooks recommended the 'discriminate and intelligent use of notes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewing institutionalized newsgathering and supported fact-centered reporting. Controversies/anti-patterns: reliance on collusion with publicity seekers, overreliance on memory instead of notes (earlier norms), and professional prohibitions (e.g., AP prohibition on interviews until 1926). Evaluate whether interviews are conducted to inform vs. to promote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraph/wire-service influence on news style (hypothesis and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common argument is that telegraphy and wire services promoted terse, value-free reporting and reduced bias by imposing stylistic and economic constraints on prose and transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents Shaw and Carey’s telegraph/wire-service hypothesis but critiques its sufficiency: telegraphic constraints may explain stylistic changes but not the self-conscious moral articulation of objectivity. Empirical anomalies (timing of bias decline, uneven prose changes) mean this factor should be evaluated cautiously and not treated as a sole causal criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-partisanship / distinction from partisan press
rubrics_metrics.description: A core standard of objectivity is that newspapers and journalists should not be declared allies or agents of political parties; objective journalists avoid presenting news primarily from a party perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess coverage for omission, selective reporting, framing favoring one party, and explicit party advocacy. Historical anti-patterns: 19th-century partisan papers that neglected opponents’ events or described rival rallies disparagingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational culture and professionalization as enablers of objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The emergence of a distinct occupational culture among reporters — clubs, rituals, interviewing norms, pride in craft, and an identity distinct from publishers or parties — created conditions under which objectivity could be articulated and internalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether journalists identify primarily with an occupational community and audience, whether they engage in shared rituals/education, and whether such culture produces rhetoric and pedagogy that teaches objectivity to newcomers. Look for evidence of professional associations, textbooks, training curricula, and intra-occupational discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durkheimian condition: ritual solidarity (articulation via ceremonies and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulation of moral norms is encouraged by forms of ritual solidarity (e.g., annual meetings, awards banquets, induction ceremonies) that prompt group members to state explicitly the group's ways and moral rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a profession will codify a norm, look for ritual occasions that produce formal statements (codes, speeches). Such events often produce explicit articulations that become normative guides; they are occasions where occupational ideals are publicly rehearsed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durkheimian condition: cultural contact and conflict (definitional boundary-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural contact and conflict with other groups can provoke articulation of norms as a way to define the group in relation to others (claiming independence or affiliation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether external conflicts or cross-cultural interactions motivated professionals to frame distinctive norms (e.g., distinguishing journalists from public relations or party operatives). Norms can be rhetorical tools for boundary-definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weberian condition: pedagogical imperative / need to socialize trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: In large institutions where enculturation cannot take place informally, the need to train people in batches and transmit the group's ways creates a pedagogical economy leading to explicit rules and moral norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for formal schooling, textbooks, codes, and training programs that articulate rules of practice. A predictable sign of a norm's institutionalization is its incorporation into teaching and onboarding practices; beware of overlearned rigidities as an artifact of pedagogical transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weberian condition: hierarchical/political control (superiors constraining subordinates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superiors in complex organizations may formalize norms to control subordinates; political control needs can encourage the emergence and codification of formalized norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate organizational structures and managerial motives: whether formal rules serve to limit subordinate discretion and whether such rules are used instrumentally by managers. Presence of written directives, managerial codes, and enforcement mechanisms indicates this condition.
